topic: The Pi-Collision Paradox: Why Bouncing Blocks Count Digits of Pi
target_audience: High school students and undergraduate math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Setup: The Elastic Collision Problem
sections.content: Introduce the physical system: Two blocks of different masses on a frictionless surface, with a wall on the left. The smaller block is at rest, and the larger block moves toward it. Define elastic collisions (conservation of momentum and kinetic energy).
sections.example: A small block (mass m) and a large block (mass M = 100m) sliding on an ice rink. The larger block strikes the smaller one, which bounces off the wall, creating a series of 'clacks'.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Mapping to Velocity Space
sections.content: Explain that tracking x-positions is hard, but mapping velocities as coordinates (v1, v2) on a 2D plane makes collisions look like reflections. A collision with the wall is a reflection across an axis; a collision between blocks is a reflection across a specific line.
sections.example: Visual animation showing the state point (v1, v2) bouncing inside a wedge-shaped region formed by two lines intersecting at the origin.

sections.title: The Geometric Connection
sections.content: Explain the geometric insight: The angle between the two collision lines depends on the ratio of the masses. As the mass ratio M/m increases (e.g., 100, 10,000, 1,000,000), the 'wedge' gets narrower. The total number of collisions corresponds to how many times a straight line fits into this arc.
sections.example: An animation showing a circular arc with an angle θ = arctan(sqrt(m/M)). As M increases, the arc becomes a tiny slice, and the path 'bounces' along the arc like a billiard ball.

sections.title: The Grand Reveal: Digits of Pi
sections.content: Reveal the magic formula: If the mass ratio is 10^2n, the total number of collisions is exactly the first n+1 digits of pi. Connect the physics of conservation laws to the geometry of circles, which naturally yields the constant π.
sections.example: A table showing: M=m (3 collisions), M=100m (31 collisions), M=10,000m (314 collisions). Visual text appearing: 3, 31, 314...

sections.title: Conclusion and Intuition
sections.content: Summarize that 'counting' is just a discrete version of 'measuring an angle.' The collisions effectively compute the arc length of a circle, which is the definition of π.
sections.example: A final visual of the two blocks colliding, transforming into a rotating clock hand that stops precisely at the digits of π.
